hints: Look for a rigid double bond where each carbon carries two different groups, and separately look for a carbon with four different single-bonded groups.
walkthrough:
Spot where cis-trans can happen**
Think about what stops rotation. Single bonds rotate freely, so they cannot lock two arrangements. A C=C double bond locks the geometry because the pi bond prevents rotation. In Q the only such site is the trisubstituted alkene in the right hand fragment, $CH_3-C(H)=C$, where each C of the double bond has two different substituents. That is the group to circle.

Spot where optical isomerism comes from**
Picture a carbon with four different things attached. That carbon is tetrahedral and has no plane of symmetry, so its mirror image cannot be superimposed. In Q this is the saturated $CH$ carbon in the middle of the ester acid chain, bonded to H, to $CH_2CHO$, to $CH(CHO)$ via the alkene side and to $CH_2CO_2R$. Mark that carbon with *.
Final answer: Circle the C=C alkene group in Q. Mark with * the chiral carbon atom in the acid-derived fragment (the saturated carbon bonded to four different groups).

hints: Think about shaking a solute with two liquids that do not mix and waiting until no further net transfer occurs.
Recall whether K(partition) compares masses, volumes or concentrations, and what condition must be stated for the ratio to be constant.
walkthrough:
Picture the experiment**
Imagine Q shaken with hexane and methanol which do not mix. Q dissolves in both to some extent and moves between the layers until the rate moving one way equals the rate moving back.

Define the constant**
At that dynamic equilibrium at constant temperature, the ratio of the concentration of Q in solvent 1 to the concentration of Q in solvent 2 is constant. That ratio is $K_{partition}$, for example $K_{partition} = [Q]_{hexane}/[Q]_{methanol}$.
Final answer: Partition coefficient is the ratio of the concentrations of a solute dissolved in two immiscible solvents (or liquids) at equilibrium.

hints: Work out how much Q is left in the methanol layer and then convert both masses to concentrations using the correct layer volumes.
Set up the ratio concentration in hexane divided by concentration in methanol, checking that both concentrations use the same mass and volume units.
walkthrough:
Find what is left behind**
Start with $0.25$ g total. $0.060$ g moves into hexane, so methanol keeps $0.25 - 0.060 = 0.19$ g. A common slip is to divide $0.25$ by $10.0$, forgetting that some solute has left.

Convert to concentrations**
Concentration means mass per unit volume in the same layer:
$$[Q]_{hexane} = \frac{0.060}{40.0} = 0.00150 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$$
$$[Q]_{methanol} = \frac{0.25-0.060}{10.0} = \frac{0.19}{10.0} = 0.0190 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$$
Volumes must stay with their own layer, $40.0$ $\text{cm}^3$ for hexane and $10.0$ $\text{cm}^3$ for methanol.

Take the ratio**
$$K_{partition} = \frac{[Q]_{hexane}}{[Q]_{methanol}} = \frac{0.00150}{0.0190} = 0.0789 \approx 0.079$$
If you define it the other way round, $K_{partition} = 0.0190/0.00150 \approx 12.7$. Either is accepted if your definition is clear. The small value shows Q prefers methanol to hexane.

Final answer: Concentration in hexane $= 0.060/40.0 = 0.00150$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$
Concentration in methanol $= (0.25-0.060)/10.0 = 0.0190$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$
$K_{partition} = (0.060/40.0)/(0.19/10.0) = 0.079$ for hexane/methanol (12.7 for the reverse ratio).

hints: List all reactive sites in Q: phenol ring, C=C alkene, two aldehydes, and an ester linkage, before considering any reagent.
Recall what excess aqueous bromine does separately to an isolated alkene and to a phenol with free 2,4,6 positions.
Recall which carbonyl groups NaBH4 can reduce and which it leaves untouched under normal conditions.
Think about which protons hot excess NaOH will remove and which ester bond it will cleave.
Count how many products form in the hydrolysis and what happens to the aldehyde and alkene groups in base.
Match each transformation to its reaction type: addition, substitution, reduction, hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Map the functional groups**
Hold Q in your mind as four reactive regions: a phenol $HO-C_6H_4-$, an ester $-CH_2CH_2-O-CO-CH_2-$, an alkene $-C(CH_3)=CH-$, and two aldehydes $-CHO$. Each reagent picks out different regions, so work reagent by reagent.

Excess bromine water does two jobs**
First, the alkene undergoes electrophilic addition. The $Br-Br$ bond polarises, $Br^{+}$ adds to form a bromonium ion, then $Br^{-}$ opens it to give $-C(Br)-C(Br)-$. The C=C disappears. Second, the phenol ring is hugely activated by the $-OH$ group toward electrophilic substitution. With excess $Br_2$, substitution occurs at both available ortho positions, 2 and 6 relative to $OH$ (para is blocked by the side chain), giving a 2,6-dibromophenol unit plus $HBr$. So the product contains three new $Br_2$ units in total: one added, two substituted.

Borohydride is selective**
$NaBH_4$ is a gentle hydride donor, $H^{-}$. It attacks the polar $C=O$ of aldehydes very easily to give after work up a primary alcohol:
$$R-CHO + [H] \rightarrow R-CH_2OH$$
Both aldehydes in Q react, so you get a diol with two $-CH_2OH$ groups. It is not strong enough to reduce C=C or the ester under these conditions, and it does not touch the phenol. Draw Q unchanged except $-CHO$ replaced by $-CH_2OH$.

Hot excess alkali hydrolyses and neutralises**
Hot $NaOH(aq)$ cleaves the ester by alkaline hydrolysis (saponification):
$$RCO_2R' + NaOH \rightarrow RCO_2^{-}Na^{+} + R'OH$$
Here $R'$ is $HO-C_6H_4-CH_2CH_2-$, so you liberate 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)phenol. In excess base its phenolic $OH$ is also deprotonated to the phenoxide, $Na^{+} {}^{-}O-C_6H_4-CH_2CH_2OH$. The acid fragment becomes the sodium carboxylate, $Na^{+} {}^{-}O_2C-CH_2-CH(CH_2CHO)-C(CH_3)=CH-CHO$. Aldehydes do not undergo Cannizzaro under these dilute conditions in the scheme, and the C=C is unchanged.

Name the reaction types**
Bromine addition to C=C is electrophilic addition, bromination of the ring is electrophilic substitution. Hydride attack on aldehyde is reduction, often described as nucleophilic addition. Ester cleavage with $NaOH$ is hydrolysis (also acid-base neutralisation for the phenol). Listing all three correctly earns the final mark.

Final answer: With excess $\text{Br}_{2}(aq)$: dibromo addition product across the C=C ($-C(Br)-C(Br)-$) plus 2,6-dibromination of the phenol ring (Br at both ortho positions to OH).
With $\text{NaBH}_{4}$: both $-CHO$ reduced to $-CH_{2}OH$ (primary alcohol), C=C, ester and phenol unchanged.
With excess hot $\text{NaOH}(aq)$: $HO-C_{6}H_{4}-CH_{2}CH_{2}OH$ as its phenoxide $Na^{+} {}^{-}O-C_{6}H_{4}-CH_{2}CH_{2}OH$ plus the carboxylate $Na^{+} {}^{-}O_{2}C-CH_{2}-CH(CH_{2}CHO)-C(CH_{3})=CH-CHO$, aldehydes and C=C unchanged.
Types: electrophilic addition and electrophilic substitution (Br2), reduction (nucleophilic addition) (NaBH4), hydrolysis (NaOH).

hints: Compare a laboratory synthesis that creates a chiral centre without chiral control with an enzyme controlled natural synthesis.
walkthrough:
Link synthesis to optical activity**
When you make a chiral centre in the lab from achiral starting materials, both mirror image forms form in equal amounts. Their rotations cancel, so the product is a racemate with no net rotation. In nature, enzymes are chiral catalysts and make only one enantiomer, which is optically active. That is why synthetic Q and natural Q differ.
Final answer: The synthetic sample is a racemic mixture (equal mixture of enantiomers) and is optically inactive, whereas olive oil contains only one optical isomer / enantiomer of Q.
